namespace LO.IntProp.Dialectica

open Formula

inductive Player
  | w : Player
  | c : Player

abbrev Argument : Player → Formula α → Type
  | _, ⊤        => Unit
  | _, ⊥        => Unit
  | .w, .atom _ => Unit
  | .c, .atom _ => Unit
  | .w, φ ⋏ ψ   => Argument .w φ × Argument .w ψ
  | .c, φ ⋏ ψ   => Argument .c φ ⊕ Argument .c ψ
  | .w, φ ⋎ ψ   => Argument .w φ ⊕ Argument .w ψ
  | .c, φ ⋎ ψ   => Argument .c φ × Argument .c ψ
  | .w, ∼φ      => Argument .w φ → Argument .c φ
  | .c, ∼φ      => Argument .w φ
  | .w, φ ➝ ψ   => (Argument .w φ → Argument .w ψ) × (Argument .w φ → Argument .c ψ → Argument .c φ)
  | .c, φ ➝ ψ   => Argument .w φ × Argument .c ψ

abbrev Witness (φ : Formula α) := Argument .w φ

abbrev Counter (φ : Formula α) := Argument .c φ

def Interpret (V : α → Prop) : (φ : Formula α) → Witness φ → Counter φ → Prop
  | ⊤,       (),       ()      => True
  | ⊥,       (),       ()      => False
  | .atom a, (),       ()      => V a
  | φ ⋏ _,   ⟨θ₁, _⟩,  .inl π₁ => Interpret V φ θ₁ π₁
  | _ ⋏ ψ,   ⟨_, θ₂⟩,  .inr π₂ => Interpret V ψ θ₂ π₂
  | φ ⋎ _,   .inl θ₁,  ⟨π₁, _⟩ => Interpret V φ θ₁ π₁
  | _ ⋎ ψ,   .inr θ₂,  ⟨_, π₂⟩ => Interpret V ψ θ₂ π₂
  | ∼φ,      f,        θ       => ¬Interpret V φ θ (f θ)
  | φ ➝ ψ,   ⟨f, g⟩,   ⟨θ, π⟩  => Interpret V φ θ (g θ π) → Interpret V ψ (f θ) π

def Valid (φ : Formula α) : Prop := ∃ w, ∀ V c, ⟦w | c⟧⊩[V] φ

def NotValid (φ : Formula α) : Prop := ∀ w, ∃ V c, ¬⟦w | c⟧⊩[V] φ

scoped notation "⊩ " φ => Valid φ

scoped notation "⊮ " φ => NotValid φ

lemma not_valid_iff_notValid {φ : Formula α} : (¬⊩ φ) ↔ (⊮ φ) := by
  simp [Valid, NotValid]

@[simp] lemma interpret_verum {w c V} : ⟦w | c⟧⊩[V] (⊤ : Formula α) := trivial

@[simp] lemma interpret_falsum {w c V} : ¬⟦w | c⟧⊩[V] (⊥ : Formula α) := id

@[simp] lemma interpret_atom {w c V} {a : α} : (⟦w | c⟧⊩[V] .atom a) ↔ V a := Eq.to_iff rfl

@[simp] lemma interpret_and_left {φ ψ : Formula α} {V θ π} :
    ⟦θ | .inl π⟧⊩[V] φ ⋏ ψ ↔ ⟦θ.1 | π⟧⊩[V] φ := Eq.to_iff rfl

@[simp] lemma interpret_and_right {φ ψ : Formula α} {V θ π} :
    ⟦θ | .inr π⟧⊩[V] φ ⋏ ψ ↔ ⟦θ.2 | π⟧⊩[V] ψ := Eq.to_iff rfl

@[simp] lemma interpret_or_left {φ ψ : Formula α} {V θ π} :
    ⟦.inl θ | π⟧⊩[V] φ ⋎ ψ ↔ ⟦θ | π.1⟧⊩[V] φ := Eq.to_iff rfl

@[simp] lemma interpret_or_right {φ ψ : Formula α} {V θ π} :
    ⟦.inr θ | π⟧⊩[V] φ ⋎ ψ ↔ ⟦θ | π.2⟧⊩[V] ψ := Eq.to_iff rfl

@[simp] lemma interpret_not {φ : Formula α} {V θ f} :
    ⟦f | θ⟧⊩[V] ∼φ ↔ ¬⟦θ | f θ⟧⊩[V] φ := Eq.to_iff rfl

@[simp] lemma interpret_imply {φ ψ : Formula α} {V f π} :
    ⟦f | π⟧⊩[V] φ ➝ ψ ↔ (⟦π.1 | f.2 π.1 π.2⟧⊩[V] φ → ⟦f.1 π.1 | π.2⟧⊩[V] ψ) := Eq.to_iff rfl

lemma NotValid.em (a : α) : ⊮ atom a ⋎ ∼atom a := by

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a

/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

/--
The identity function. `id` takes an implicit argument `α : Sort u`
(a type in any universe), and an argument `a : α`, and returns `a`.

Although this may look like a useless function, one application of the identity
function is to explicitly put a type on an expression. If `e` has type `T`,
and `T'` is definitionally equal to `T`, then `@id T' e` typechecks, and Lean
knows that this expression has type `T'` rather than `T`. This can make a
difference for typeclass inference, since `T` and `T'` may have different
typeclass instances on them. `show T' from e` is sugar for an `@id T' e`
expression.
-/
@[inline] def id {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α := a

import Foundation.IntProp.Hilbert.Basic

/-!
  # A Toy Model of Dialectica Interpretation for Intuitionistic Propositional Logic

  ### References: https://math.andrej.com/2011/01/03/the-dialectica-interpertation-in-coq/

-/

namespace LO.IntProp.Dialectica

open Formula

inductive Player
  | w : Player
  | c : Player

abbrev Argument : Player → Formula α → Type
  | _, ⊤        => Unit
  | _, ⊥        => Unit
  | .w, .atom _ => Unit
  | .c, .atom _ => Unit
  | .w, φ ⋏ ψ   => Argument .w φ × Argument .w ψ
  | .c, φ ⋏ ψ   => Argument .c φ ⊕ Argument .c ψ
  | .w, φ ⋎ ψ   => Argument .w φ ⊕ Argument .w ψ
  | .c, φ ⋎ ψ   => Argument .c φ × Argument .c ψ
  | .w, ∼φ      => Argument .w φ → Argument .c φ
  | .c, ∼φ      => Argument .w φ
  | .w, φ ➝ ψ   => (Argument .w φ → Argument .w ψ) × (Argument .w φ → Argument .c ψ → Argument .c φ)
  | .c, φ ➝ ψ   => Argument .w φ × Argument .c ψ

abbrev Witness (φ : Formula α) := Argument .w φ

abbrev Counter (φ : Formula α) := Argument .c φ

def Interpret (V : α → Prop) : (φ : Formula α) → Witness φ → Counter φ → Prop
  | ⊤,       (),       ()      => True
  | ⊥,       (),       ()      => False
  | .atom a, (),       ()      => V a
  | φ ⋏ _,   ⟨θ₁, _⟩,  .inl π₁ => Interpret V φ θ₁ π₁
  | _ ⋏ ψ,   ⟨_, θ₂⟩,  .inr π₂ => Interpret V ψ θ₂ π₂
  | φ ⋎ _,   .inl θ₁,  ⟨π₁, _⟩ => Interpret V φ θ₁ π₁
  | _ ⋎ ψ,   .inr θ₂,  ⟨_, π₂⟩ => Interpret V ψ θ₂ π₂
  | ∼φ,      f,        θ       => ¬Interpret V φ θ (f θ)
  | φ ➝ ψ,   ⟨f, g⟩,   ⟨θ, π⟩  => Interpret V φ θ (g θ π) → Interpret V ψ (f θ) π

informal_statement: For any element \( a \) in a given type, the statement \( \mathsf{atom}(a) \) is not necessarily equivalent to its negation \( \neg \mathsf{atom}(a) \).
informal_proof:
Let \( a \) be an arbitrary element of a type \( \alpha \). We aim to show that it is not necessarily the case that \( \mathsf{atom}(a) \) is equivalent to \( 
eg \mathsf{atom}(a) \).

Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that \( \mathsf{atom}(a) \) were equivalent to \( 
eg \mathsf{atom}(a) \). This would imply that \( a \) is both a member of a certain set and not a member of the same set, which is a direct contradiction. Therefore, \( \mathsf{atom}(a) \) cannot be equivalent to \( 
eg \mathsf{atom}(a) \).

Hence, neither \( \mathsf{atom}(a) \) nor its negation can hold the property \( \mathsf{atom}(a) \wedge 
eg \mathsf{atom}(a) \), proving that the statement \( \mathsf{atom}(a) \wedge 
eg \mathsf{atom}(a) \) is not valid for any \( a \).

namespace LO.IntProp.Dialectica

open Formula

inductive Player
  | w : Player
  | c : Player

abbrev Argument : Player → Formula α → Type
  | _, ⊤        => Unit
  | _, ⊥        => Unit
  | .w, .atom _ => Unit
  | .c, .atom _ => Unit
  | .w, φ ⋏ ψ   => Argument .w φ × Argument .w ψ
  | .c, φ ⋏ ψ   => Argument .c φ ⊕ Argument .c ψ
  | .w, φ ⋎ ψ   => Argument .w φ ⊕ Argument .w ψ

This bidirectional relationship underscores the foundational connection between truth and derivability in the system.

informal_statement: For any interpretation (function and variable assignments), the satisfaction of "not φ" is equivalent to the negation of the satisfaction of φ.
informal_proof:
An interpretation provides a specific assignment of truth values to atomic formulas, allowing us to determine the truth of more complex formulas like "not φ." The satisfaction of "not φ" under such an interpretation is precisely defined as the negation of the satisfaction of φ. This means:

1. **Interpretation and Satisfaction**: An interpretation assigns truth values to all atomic propositions. "not φ" modifies the atomic formula φ, asserting its opposite truth value.

2. **Equivalence via Negation**: By the definition of logical negation, if φ is satisfied (true), then "not φ" is not satisfied (false). Conversely, if φ is not satisfied (false), "not φ" is satisfied (true).

3. **Formalize the Equivalence**: Therefore, the satisfaction of "not φ" under any interpretation logically mirrors the negation of φ's satisfaction, confirming that "not φ" is equivalent to "not (satisfaction of φ)."

This equivalence is fundamental to how negation works in formal logic, ensuring consistency and coherence in logical systems.

namespace LO.IntProp.Dialectica

open Formula

inductive Player
  | w : Player
  | c : Player

abbrev Argument : Player → Formula α → Type
  | _, ⊤        => Unit
  | _, ⊥        => Unit
  | .w, .atom _ => Unit
  | .c, .atom _ => Unit
  | .w, φ ⋏ ψ   => Argument .w φ × Argument .w ψ
  | .c, φ ⋏ ψ   => Argument .c φ ⊕ Argument .c ψ
  | .w, φ ⋎ ψ   => Argument .w φ ⊕ Argument .w ψ
  | .c, φ ⋎ ψ   => Argument .c φ × Argument .c ψ
  | .w, ∼φ      => Argument .w φ → Argument .c φ
  | .c, ∼φ      => Argument .w φ
  | .w, φ ➝ ψ   => (Argument .w φ → Argument .w ψ) × (Argument .w φ → Argument .c ψ → Argument .c φ)
  | .c, φ ➝ ψ   => Argument .w φ × Argument .c ψ

abbrev Witness (φ : Formula α) := Argument .w φ

abbrev Counter (φ : Formula α) := Argument .c φ

def Interpret (V : α → Prop) : (φ : Formula α) → Witness φ → Counter φ → Prop

  | ⊥,       (),       ()      => False

informal_statement: The lemma `interpret_or_right` establishes an equivalence between two interpretations of the disjunction of two formulas, `φ ⋎ ψ`, given certain contexts. Specifically, it states that interpreting `φ ⋎ ψ` with a right context `π` is equivalent to interpreting `ψ` with the right context specifically for `π`.
informal_proof:
To prove this lemma, we start by analyzing the given equivalence:
\[ \llbracket.\text{inr}\, \theta \,|\, \pi\rrbracket \Vdash [V] \varphi \, \lif \, \psi \; \equ longleftrightarrow \; \llbracket\theta \,|\, \pi.2\rrbracket \Vdash [V] \psi \]

Breaking it down:
1. **Left-Hand Side Interpretation**: 
   - The expression \(\llbracket.\text{inr}\, \theta \,|\, \pi\rrbracket\) represents an interpretation where `θ` is taken as the right component of the context `π`.
   - Under this interpretation, the disjunction \(\varphi \, \lif \, \psi\) is evaluated, and the formula is satisfied under the given variable assignment \(V\).

2. **Right-Hand Side Interpretation**:
   - Here, the interpretation restricts to the right part of the context `π`, specifically `π.2`, and evaluates only `ψ` under \(V\).

3. **Equivalence**:
   - The lemma asserts that these two interpretations are equivalent. Essentially, the satisfaction of the disjunction under the general context where the right component is specified is the same as the direct satisfaction of the second formula in that right component context.

The proof hinges on recognizing that the left-hand side interpretation, when considering only the right part of the context, reduces to the right-hand side interpretation. Hence, both expressions evaluate to the same satisfaction status.

Therefore, the lemma simplifies the context handling for disjunctive formulas by allowing direct evaluation of the specific component under the right context.

informal_statement: In the context of forcing in model theory, interpreting a disjunction `φ ⋎ ψ` under a model where the first option is selected (i.e., `.inl θ | π`) is equivalent to simply interpreting `φ` under the model `θ | π.1`.
informal_proof: When working within a model where `.inl θ | π` is selected (which selects the left-hand side of the disjunction), the interpretation of the disjunction `φ ⋎ ψ` simplifies to just the interpretation of `φ` under a less general context (`θ | π.1`). Since in this choice, the option `ψ` is disregarded, and we only consider `φ` under the specified context, the equivalence holds by the definition of the interpretation under such forcing conditions.

When the conjunction of two formulas `φ` and `ψ` is satisfiable in a context where another context `π` is added to the right of context `θ`, then `ψ` alone is also satisfiable in a context that involves `θ` and `π`. 

In other words, if `θ | π` entails `φ ∧ ψ`, then it also entails `ψ`, considering the structure and constraints imposed by the logical framework.

1. **Understanding the Context**: The theorem is set within a logical framework that interprets and manipulates contexts (θ and π) and formulas (φ, ψ). The turnstile symbol (⊩) indicates that a formula is a semantic consequence under a given interpretation.

2. **Interpretation of Context**: The expression `θ | .inr π` suggests an operation that appends or extends the context `θ` with another context `π` on the right side. Similarly, `θ.2 | π` indicates a restructured or modified context.

3. **Conjunction Handling**: The connective `⋎` represents logical conjunction (∧). The theorem asserts that if `θ | π` entails both `φ` and `ψ` (i.e., `φ ∧ ψ`), then it also entails `ψ` within a modified context.

4. **Derivation of `ψ`**: Assuming `θ | π` entails `φ ∧ ψ`, by the nature of conjunction, both `φ` and `ψ` must individually be true under the given interpretation. Therefore, `ψ` alone must also be true in the modified context `θ.2 | π`.

5. **Conclusion**: The equivalence follows from the fact that the presence of `φ ∧ ψ` in a context entails the presence of `ψ` in a related but possibly simplified context, aligning with the principles of logical distributivity or context management in the system.

informal_proof: Given any interpretation \( \Vdash_{w|c} \) over \( V \) in the context of \( \alpha \), the formula \( \top \) represents a tautology, which is a statement that is always true regardless of the interpretation. By the definition of the satisfaction relation in formal logic, \( \top \) is trivially satisfied because it expresses the fundamental truth of the matter. Therefore, under any interpretation \( \Vdash_{w|c} \) and valuation \( V \) in \( \alpha \), the statement \( \Vdash_{w|c} (\top) \) holds true.

informal_statement: A formula $\phi$ is valid if there exists a term $w$ such that for any interpretation $V$ and context $c$, the formula $\phi$ holds in those interpretations.
informal_proof:
To understand the concept of validity, consider the definition provided: a formula $\phi$ is valid if there exists a term $w$ such that for any interpretation $V$ and context $c$, the formula $\phi$ holds true in those interpretations. This means that the truth of $\phi$ is guaranteed regardless of how we interpret the symbols in the system, as long as the structure defined by $w$, $V$, and $c$ is maintained. Essentially, validity ensures that $\phi$ is universally true across all possible domains defined by appropriate interpretations.

To further clarify, the statement asserts that for a formula to be valid, there must be a specific $w$ that serves as a universal witness, confirming $\phi$'s truth in every scenario defined by different $V$ and $c$. This aligns with the intuitive understanding of a universally valid formula in logic, which remains true no matter what interpretations are assigned to its components.

Additionally, the remarks highlight that $\phi$ does not contain any free variables, which underscores the necessity of $w$ and the control over the domain and structures involved. This substantiates that the existence of such a $w$ as a universal witness is both possible and sufficient for $\phi$'s validity.

In summary, the definition encapsulates the requirement for a formula to hold universally true across all possible interpretations, ensuring its validity in a comprehensive manner. This aligns with the standard logical notion of a formula being valid or tautologically true, which is independent of the particular interpretations given to its terms and symbols.

/--
The unit type, the canonical type with one element, named `unit` or `()`.
In other words, it describes only a single value, which consists of said constructor applied
to no arguments whatsoever.
The `Unit` type is similar to `void` in languages derived from C.

`Unit` is actually defined as `PUnit.{1}` where `PUnit` is the universe
polymorphic version. The `Unit` should be preferred over `PUnit` where possible to avoid
unnecessary universe parameters.

In functional programming, `Unit` is the return type of things that "return
nothing", since a type with one element conveys no additional information.
When programming with monads, the type `m Unit` represents an action that has
some side effects but does not return a value, while `m α` would be an action
that has side effects and returns a value of type `α`.
-/
abbrev Unit : Type := PUnit

informal_statement: The `Interpret` function provides a method to determine the truth value of a logical formula based on a given valuation of its atomic propositions, along with specified witnesses and counters. It systematically evaluates formulas by breaking them down into their constituent logical connectives and applying the corresponding rules for each type of logical operation.
informal_proof:
We will analyze how the `Interpret` function works by examining key case definitions across various logical connectives.

1. **Atomic Propositions**:
   For an atomic proposition `.atom a`, `Interpret V φ θ π` evaluates to `V a`, which is a truth value determined by the valuation `V` of the atomic proposition `a`.

2. **Conjunction (φ ∧ ψ)**:
   The interpretation of a conjunction `.inl π₁` and a separate formula is determined by applying the interpretation function recursively to the left part. This means the truth value is calculated based on the evaluation of the left formula combined with the interpretation of the right formula.

3. **Disjunction (φ ∨ ψ)**:
   The interpretation of a disjunction `.inr π₂` depends solely on the evaluation of the right formula. This provides a straightforward mechanism to assess the truth value of the right-hand side.

4. **Negation (∼φ)**:
   The negation of a formula flips its interpretation. If `Interpret V φ θ π` evaluates to `True`, then `∼φ` will evaluate to `False`, and vice versa, ensuring that negation behaves as expected.

5. **Implication (φ ➝ ψ)**:
   The interpretation of an implication involves the evaluation of the left formula combined with the interpretation of the right formula. Specifically, `Interpret V φ θ π` yields `True` if the left formula is interpreted as `True` and the right formula, with a modified witness, is interpreted as `True`.

By methodically applying these case definitions to any given formula, the `Interpret` function ensures that the truth value of the formula is accurately determined based on the provided valuation and the logical structure of the formula itself. This systematic approach validates the correctness of the `Interpret` function in capturing the intended logical semantics.
